# Geographic Trends in Opioid and Polysubstance Overdose Deaths in the US, 2014–2023

KEY WORDS:  opioid; mortality; geographic trend

J Gen Intern Med 40(15):3804–7 DOI: 10.1007/s11606-025-09589-1 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Society of General Internal Medicine 2025

## INTRODUCTION

The opioid overdose crisis in the US has intensified over four distinct waves, with the most recent wave marked by a rise in fentanyl-cocaine co-involvement in the Northeastern US and fentanyl-methamphetamine co-involvement in the Western US through 2021.1 In May 2024, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) announced that for the first time since 2018, the US experienced a national decline in the rate of drug overdose deaths, with decreases as large as 30% in some states.2 However, little is currently known about geographic variations in this shift in opioid-related mortality, particularly as it relates to fentanyl and polysubstance overdose. The goal of this study was to examine regional trends in opioid overdose mortality overall and in combination with other substances up to 2023.

## METHODS

We conducted a serial cross-sectional study using data from the CDC Wide-Ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research database from 2014 to 2023. We report opioid overdose death rates per 100,000 population, ageadjusted to the 2000 US Census population, identified using International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision cause-of-death codes (Table 1).1 Descriptive trends were assessed across US Census Bureau regions for all opioid overdose deaths including those attributed to a synthetic opioid and another co-involved substance. Given reports of diverging mortality in the Western US from similar trends in other regions, we focused our analyses on West and non-West (i.e., Northeast, South, and Midwest) comparisons. Institutional Review Board approval was not required due to the use of publicly available,

deidentified data. All analyses were conducted using R version 4.3.2. The study followed the STROBE reporting guideline.

## RESULTS

Overall opioid overdose mortality in the US increased from 9.04 to 25.01 per 100,000 population between 2014 and 2022. Between 2022 and 2023, opioid overdose mortality in the West continued to rise by 14.1% (2.85 per 100,000 population) while mortality in non- West regions decreased by 7.5% over the same period (1.99 per 100,000 population) (Fig. 1, Table 1). In the West, synthetic opioid overdose deaths increased by 19.4% between 2022 and 2023 (3.41 per 100,000 population) while synthetic opioid overdose deaths decreased by 6.6% (1.59 per 100,000 population) across non-West regions over the same period. Beginning in 2019, rates of synthetic opioid-stimulant co-involved overdose deaths accelerated across all regions. Between 2022 and 2023, cocaine was more commonly detected among co-involved overdoses in non-West regions and increased there by 4.3%, while non-cocaine psychostimulants were more commonly detected in the West and increased there by 31.6%. Additionally, from 2014 to 2023, the proportion of synthetic opioid-related deaths involving cocaine increased from 12.4 to 35.4% in non-West regions and from 3.3 to 14.1% in the West. Over the same period, the proportion of synthetic opioid-related deaths involving other psychostimulants increased from 4.1 to 25.7% in non-West regions and from 11.8 to 52.2% in the West.

## DISCUSSION

The continued increase in opioid overdose deaths in the West, masked by a decline in mortality nationally, underscores an ongoing shift in the landscape of the overdose crisis. Our findings are consistent with earlier reports of an increase in state-level fentanyl-related deaths in jurisdictions west of the Mississippi River, which estimated a 3-year lag in fentanyl-related mortality in western states compared to their eastern counterparts.3 Available data suggest that this shift was more likely driven by changes in fentanyl supply rather than demand, with

Rates of co-involved opioid and stimulant overdose death have increased over the past decade, with approximately one in three fentanyl-related deaths now involving cocaine in non-West regions and approximately one in two now involving other psychostimulants (largely methamphetamine) in the West. The emergence of these distinct overdose patterns highlights the need for ongoing surveillance of these substances in local drug markets, low-barrier and equitable access to medications for opioid use disorder, and investment from payors and investigators

in behavioral therapies and off-label pharmacotherapy for stimulant use disorder.5,6

Study limitations include reliance on death certificates to identify overdose deaths and potential state-level variation in death investigation systems and mortality reporting.
